- (lines 596-599): “In both young and aged mice, inhibiting the secretion of IL-17a through Y320 effectively alleviated OE damage, respiratory epithelial metaplasia, and olfactory dysfunction caused by Met injury. These changes were even more pronounced in aged mice”. The statement is not justified by the research findings, in the case of “even more pronounced in aged mice”. Research findings suggest instead a similar effect on aged and young mice.
2. Equally, in the organoid studies reported in Figure 4, there is an age effect and there is an effect of the Th17 coculture but without an obvious interaction, leading to additive functional effects rather than age specific effects.
- (lines 608-609): “we effectively restored neuronal differentiation and inhibited the metaplasia of Krt19+ respiratory epithelial cells in aged organoids”. This Is just partially justified, since the effect on young organoids is similar (fig 4G-I).
3. An additional concern is related to the compound Y320. The authors justify the use of this compound as a selective tool to reduce IL17 secretion by T cells, but the available literature indicates a much broader mode of action of this drug.
4. In Figure 1, why were the data not analysed as one dataset? It appears that the young and old datasets are analysed separately. This is in contrast to the data shown in Figure 2, in which the data are analysed as one pooled cluster of cells. The approach in Figure 2 appears to be the right one.
Minor comments
1. Page 4 the sentence “Due….condition” (line 50-52) is missing a reference. How can loss of smell be fatal?
2. The 3rd paragraph of the introduction contains many abbreviations. An example is the sentence “When…regeneration” (line 71-74). To the broader scientific readership this will be very difficult to read and it is recommended that these abbreviations are written in full to avoid confusion.
3. Introduction last paragraph. Suggest to write as hypothesis/aim rather than a summary of findings.
4. Out of curiosity, did the authors also analyse olfactory receptor mRNA expression as a function of age and IL17 interventions?
5. Figure 3G and 3I: were there any changes in organoid size or morohology?

confined to the lamina propria. This redistribution pattern aligns with observations in
young versus aged OE (revised Figure 1g-i). These results provided direct
experimental validation of the CellChat-predicted downregulation of the
Mif/CD74-CD44 interaction axis unpon IL-17a ablation (revised Figure S7g-h; page
32-33,lines 683-691).
Together, these new data strengthened our conclusion that IL-17a deficiency
attenuates olfactory inflammation partly by suppressing this key ligand-receptor
pathway, thereby helping preserve olfactory function in aging. Corresponding images
are presented inResponseFigure1below.

Reviewer#2(Remarks totheAuthor):
This study investigates the impact of age-related inflammation (inflamm-aging)
on the homeostasis and regeneration of the olfactory epithelium (OE), focusing
on the role of interleukin-17a. The results indicate that IL-17a expression
increases in aged OE, activating immune cells and promoting interactions
between horizontal basal cells (HBCs) and T cells, leading to inflammatory
signaling and olfactory dysfunction.Administration of the IL-17a inhibitorY320
enhanced olfactory nerve regeneration and suppressed age-related abnormal
changes in OE, such as respiratory epithelialization. Additionally, co-culturing
OE organoids with Th17 cells inhibited neurogenesis and facilitated the
transformation of OE into respiratory epithelium, an effect that was alleviated
by IL-17a-neutralizing antibodies. T cell-specific knockout of IL-17a promoted
HBC mobilization and differentiation into globose basal cells, enhancing OE
regeneration. These findings suggest that IL-17a plays a crucial role in
age-related olfactory dysfunction and highlight the potential of IL-17a-targeted
therapies fortreating olfactory impairments inaging.
While the study suggests the importance of Th17 cells in olfactory impairments
in aging, several important experiments are required to strengthen the
hypothesis. There were several concerns regarding the support for the authors’
hypothesisas described below:
Comments inno specificorder:
1. Why doTh17 cells increase in OE as aging?The molecularmechanism should
be mentioned. For example, cytokines such as IL-23 and IL-6 and chemokines to
recruitTh17shouldbeexamined in detail.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this critical question regarding the
mechanism underlying the age-associated accumulation ofTh17 cells in OE.
The increase in Th17 cells in aged OE is driven by a pro-inflammatory
microenvironment resulting from both systemic immunosenescence and local tissue
alterations. Systemically, aging is associated with a chronic, low-grade systemic
inflammation state known as inflammaging, which senescent cells release factors like
IL-6 and IL-1β via the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP).Within the
local OE tissue, resident innate immune cells such as macrophages and dendritic cells
become persistently activated, leading to sustained production of key polarizing
cytokines, including IL-23, IL-6, IL-1β, and TGF-β. This cytokine milieu promotes
Th17 differentiation and maintenance. Furthermore, IL-17 secretion from established
Th17 cells can induce chemokines like CCL20, creating a self-amplifying
inflammatory loop that recruits moreimmunecells and reinforces the response5,6.
Our initial data (Figure S1E) confirmed a general upregulation of inflammatory
mediators, including T cell recruitment (Cxcl10, Cxcl16), NF-κB targets
(Tnf, Il6, Cxcl5), as well as TNF superfamily members (Tnfrsf1a, Tnfsf10) in the
aged OE.
Guided by the reviewer’s suggestion, we have now expanded investigation into key
pathways involved in Th17 chemotaxis recruitment, co-stimulatory molecules,
maintenance, and polarization 7. Our new analysis revealed that the aged OE
microenvironment exhibits upregulated expression of several chemokines, including
Ccl20, Cxcl10, Ccl2, and Ccl7, along with their corresponding receptors (Ccr6, Cxcr3,
Ccr2), which are critical for Th17 recruitment. In addition, cytokines central to Th17
polarization and maintenance, such as Il6, Il23a, Il1b, Tgfb1, and Tnf, were
significantly increased in aged OE tissues, along with elevated expression of key
transcription factors (Stat3, Rorc, Batf). Several of these are NF-κB target genes, and
members of TNF receptor/ligand superfamily remained upregulated (revised Figure
S1k; pages 10-11,lines 193-208).
To further validate these findings at the protein level, we performed ELISA and
confirmed that both IL-17a and IL-23 were significantly elevated in aged OE tissue
homogenates and plasma(revised Figure 2i; page12,lines 234-236).
Together, these new results delineated a model in which the aged OE exhibits a
pro-inflammatory microenvironment characterized byenhanced chemotacticsignaling,
antigen presentation, and polarizing cytokine production, collectively facilitating the
recruitment, local expansion,and stabilization ofTh17 cells.
The corresponding images are presented in Response Figure 10 below. We are
grateful to the reviewer for this insightful suggestion, which has substantially
strengthened themechanisticscope of ourstudy.

2. What antigens activate Th17 cells in the olfactory epithelium? Are there
differences inTCRrepertoireascompared toTh17cells in othertissues?
Response:
We sincerely appreciate the reviewer for raising these critical questions regarding the
antigenicdrivers andTCRrepertoire ofTh17 cells intheolfactory epithelium.
For the first question, the OE represents a unique immunological interface due to its
direct and continuous exposure to the external environment. Previous studies have
demonstrated that intranasal infections preferentially induce Th17 cells responses 8 .
Th17 cells in OE are primarily activated by airborne microbial antigens derived from
commensal bacteria, fungi, and pathogens, such as Streptococcus pyogenes present in
the nasal environment 9.Antigen presentation in the OE is mediated by dendritic cells
and other immune cells such as eosinophils. These activated Th17 cells produce
cytokines including IL-17,which contributes to host defense against pathogens.
To systematically evaluate the potential antigenic drivers in our model, we analyzed
scRNA-seq data from the OE of young and aged mice. We first subset CD4+ cells
from the T cell population and subsequently identified Th17 cells based on gene set
scoring. The Th17 cells were predominantly abundant in aged tissues (Response
Figure 11a, b). We then manually curated four effector gene modules representing
distinct immunological pathways: Fungal-Th17 Axis, Bacterial-TLR/NOD Axis,
antiviral Type I Interferon ISGAxis, as well as Th2-STAT6Axis.The related genes in
each axis were displayed in Response Figure 11e 10, 11, 12. Module scoring analysis
revealed that the Fungal-Th17 pathway was the most highly enriched in these cells,
followed by theViral module, while the Bacterial andTh2 modules showed lower and
more restricted activity (Response Figure 11c). Therefore, we speculated that due to
the direct exposure of the OE to air containing abundant fungal spores, aging may
lead to reduced mucus secretion, impaired ciliary function, or diminished immune
clearance capacity. This could result in increased exposure to fungal antigens or
inadequate clearance. It was also reported that fungal and bacterial biofilms are
commonly found in CRS and may support chronic and recalcitrant CRS infection 13.
Thus, the persistent activation of Th17 cells and related inflammatory pathways
(particularly the Fungal-Th17 Axis) in the OE of aged mice is likely closely
etiologically linked to age-related olfactory dysfunction. Based on the analysis of data
from CKO and Flox mice at 7 and 14 dpi, we observed high expression of
fungi-related genes in Flox mice at 7 dpi (Response Figure 11d), further
demonstrating that nasal mucosa becomes more susceptible to fungal invasion under
injury conditions.
For the second question, based on the literature and our findings, we discovered
significant differences exist in the TCR repertoire of Th17 cells in the OE compared
to other tissues, such as gut and skin. Primarily driven by tissue-specific antigen
exposure, unique cytokine and dendritic cell microenvironments, and functional
specialization, OE Th17 TCR are shaped by airborne antigens (e.g., fungal spores and
commensal/pathogenic bacteria like Streptococcus pyogenes), while gut Th17 TCR
are selected by intestinal commensals (e.g., segmented filamentous bacteria) and skin
Th17 TCR recognize cutaneous microbes (e.g., Staphylococcus epidermidis). These
antigenic differences are reinforced by distinct cytokine signals and DC subsets: OE
Th17 differentiation depends on TGF-β1 and IL-6 from CD301b⁺ DCs in cervical
lymph nodes, whereas gut Th17 development relies on IL-1β and IL-23 (often
TGF-β1-independent) from CX₃CR1⁺ macrophages or CD103⁺ DC, and skin Th17
polarization requires IL-1β , IL-6, and IL-23 from dermal DC or Langerhans cells.
Consequently, TCR divergence correlates with tissue-specific homing receptors and
effector functions 14, 15, 16. Our single-cell data further showed enrichment of
Fungal-Th17 Axis genes (Clec7a, Syk, Il17a/f) in OE Th17 cells, suggesting clonal
expansions distinct from other tissues. Thus, the TCR repertoire of OE Th17 cells is
uniquely adapted to airborne challenges, highlighting the compartmentalization of
mucosal immunity. However, due to the technical limitation, we couldn’t get more
detailed information aboutTCR repertoire.Weappreciated the reviewer that provide a
new direction for our future studies, and will directly compare TCR sequences across
tissues usingsingle-cell RNA/TCRsequencing to validatethesedifferences.

3. Which cells express IL-17Ra in the olfactory epithelium? Is it expressed only

Response:
We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's insightful comment regarding the cellular
specificity of IL-17ra expressionpatterns in OE.
To precisely identify which cell types express Il17ra in OE, we performed extensive
immunofluorescence co-staining using an IL-17ra-specific antibody on OE tissues
from young and aged mice, in combination with neuronal marker Tuj1 and basal cell
marker Icam1. Our findings revealed that Il17ra expression exhibits distinct cell-type
specificity and spatiotemporal dynamics. In young mice, IL-17ra was primarily
expressed in neurons, with approximately 87.6% of the signal co-localizing with
Tuj1+ neurons in the dorsal region. In aged mice, however, the expression pattern
shifted markedly, showing strong enrichment in the basal cell layer of the dorsal
regions, where about 60% co-localized with Icam1+ basal cells. Further regional
analysis indicated that in the medial OE of aged mice, a higher proportion of Il7ra
co-localized with neurons, while in the respiratory epithelium (RE) region, expression
remained predominantly inthebasal layer across bothage groups.
Quantitative analysis confirmed that Il17ra was most abundant in neurons of young
mice but became significantly elevated in HBC of aged OE, demonstrating an
age-dependent redistribution of IL-17 signaling potential within the tissue (revised
Figure S1i, j, pages 9-10, lines 175-192). Representative images are also present in
ResponseFigure12.
In summary,the cellular landscape of IL-17ra expression is bothspecific and dynamic,
transitioningfrom neuronal dominanceto basal cells prevalence withage.

4. Obesity has also been reported to increase immune system aging and augment
Th17cells. Does obesity alsohasten olfactory epithelialdysfunction?
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this insightful question concerning the
potential link between obesity, accelerated immune aging, and olfactory dysfunction.
We agree that obesity, as a state of chronic systemic inflammation and metabolic
dysregulation, represents aplausiblefactorin hastening age-related olfactory decline.
Previous studies have established that obesity-associated chronic inflammation
contributes significantly to the pathogenesis of metabolic diseases. Among T helper
subsets, Th17 cells are known to promote autoimmune disorders 17. Furthermore,
clinical evidence indicated impaired insulin signaling, common in obesity, can affect
odor perception at the level of olfactory epithelium. Indeed, olfactory dysfunction,
ranging from mild impairment to complete anosmia, has been reported in patients
withobesity and type 2diabetes, substantiallyimpacting quality oflife18,19.
While direct mechanistic studies linking obesity and OE dysfunction remain limited,
our data provided compelling preliminary support for this connection.
Specifically, single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of young and aged OE revealed
profound dysregulation of genes related to adipocyte differentiation in aged tissue.
We observed significant upregulation of both positive (GO: 0045600) and negative
(GO: 0045599) regulators of fat cell differentiation, along with elevated expression of
key adipogenesis-related marker genes in aged OE (Response Figure 13a-d). These
findings suggested that the aged OE underwent a form of metabolic reprogramming
resembling aspects ofthesystemic metabolicdisturbance occured inobesity.
Based onthese findings, we propose a hypothesis that obesity-related systemic factors,
such as elevated free fatty acids and pro-inflammatory cytokines, may accelerate the
formation of pro-adipogenic and pro-inflammatory microenvironment within the OE.
This process could exacerbate Th17-driven inflammation and promote premature
olfactory functional decline, suggesting that aging and obesity may converge through
shared pathogenic pathways in OE.
We once again thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. Inspired by the
reviewer’s question, we consider this an important new direction for future research.
We plan to directly test this hypothesis using a diet-induced obesity mouse model to
evaluate whether obesity accelerates the expansion of Th17 cells, impairs olfactory
epithelial regeneration, and compromises olfactory function.
